source.title: The Law of Multi-Model Collaboration: Scaling Limits of Model Ensembling for Large Language Models
source.authors: Dakuan Lu; Jiaqi Zhang; Cheng Yuan; Jia-Wei Shao; Chi Zhang; Xue-Long Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures loss scaling against parameter count using a different setup from the original single-model training sweeps: pretrained model pools, Pareto frontiers, and an idealized oracle ensemble.
record.gate_note: The reported fitted loss curves and parameters are results, so they are recorded below. The study does not test scaling with training tokens or compute, validate predictions from small runs against much larger runs, or evaluate downstream tasks. Its ensemble results use an oracle that selects the lowest-loss model per text and is explicitly not a realizable inference-time system.
record.test_reason: Only the single-model frontier (R1) tests V1. It fits held-out text loss against parameter count for 12 Pareto-optimal public base models, using a different method from controlled training sweeps. The other rows describe oracle ensembles, which are a different kind of system.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is essentially correct. The authors conclude that oracle ensembles follow power-law scaling in total parameters, with an exponent similar to single models (α≈0.35) but a 43% lower fitted floor. They also conclude that cross-family diversity gives lower floors than same-family pairs. They stress that these are theoretical upper bounds from an unrealizable oracle.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than training controlled model runs across parameter, token, or compute scales, the study evaluates a pool of pretrained base models and fits Pareto-frontier losses against aggregated parameters. Ensemble loss is defined by a per-text minimum-loss oracle; ensembles are explored with iterative Pareto pruning.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported fitted parameters differ across frontier composition (single models, all ensembles, same-family pairs, and cross-family pairs). The paper also states that fitted parameters depend on model-pool makeup and that alternative loss normalizations may be appropriate; it does not experimentally vary those choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle ensembles of up to 71 pretrained models fit a power law in summed parameters (α=0.3502), with a fitted floor of 1.25 versus 2.21 for single models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oracle multi-model ensemble loss follows a power law in aggregated parameter count, with a lower asymptotic floor than single-model scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-family oracle pairs reach a lower fitted floor (2.04) than same-family pairs (2.23), which have a steeper exponent (0.85 vs 0.55).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-family diversity changes the oracle loss-scaling frontier of pair ensembles.

record.problems: The ensemble result is an explicitly unrealizable per-text oracle bound. The study uses iterative Pareto pruning, which it acknowledges may miss optimal configurations. Fitted parameters depend on the model pool, and no uncertainty intervals are reported. The held-out dataset size and detailed composition are not stated in the text provided.
record.rows_left_out: None of the separately reported scaling-fit results were left out.

untested.parts: Scaling with tokens or compute. No control showing data or compute are not bottlenecks; the frontier spans only about 0–80B parameters across mixed families.
All: no extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
All: no controlled shape variation at fixed parameter count.
All: the paper only states (Sec 6.4) that fitted parameters depend on pool makeup; it does not vary fitting choices for single-model laws.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V7 support is dropped. Differences between ensemble-composition fits are not evidence about fitting or setup choices for single-model laws, and the pool-dependence statement (Sec 6.4) is asserted, not tested. The ensemble results are a new construct (oracle collaboration) and are moved to fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss scaling with parameter count only. It does not test scaling with tokens or compute, or vary those quantities to establish that they are not bottlenecks. The ensemble results are oracle losses, not losses from a deployable collaborative system.
No validation of predictions fitted on small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or estimate of compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
The paper compares same-family and cross-family oracle pair ensembles, not controlled changes to depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count for individual models.
Only language-model text loss is studied; no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study reports differences across model-pool/frontier compositions, but does not vary fitting method, parameter counting, training schedule, or data; it does not report curves bending away from a power law or test why published studies disagree.

rows.subject: Single-model frontier (12 Pareto-optimal models selected from 71 base models)
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss against parameter count on the Pareto-optimal single-model frontier using nonlinear least squares in the original loss domain.

conditions.value: fixed held-out text dataset sampled from D
text-level summed token cross-entropy normalized by average token sequence length across models and test texts
L(P) = A P^-α + L∞; nonlinear least squares in original loss domain

rows.note: The paper describes the frontier as exhibiting a clear power-law relationship. The fitted law is Lsingle(P) = 1.11/P^0.3578 + 2.21.
rows.check: Should link to V1 only. A single frontier fit cannot show the fit-dependence V7 describes. The frontier mixes model families trained on uncontrolled token counts, and no goodness-of-fit or uncertainty is reported. The baseline is correctly 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Multi-model ensemble frontier (3,146 Pareto-optimal ensembles)
rows.size_stated: Aggregated parameter count P in billions
rows.stage_stated: pretrained base models (pre-alignment), combined using an idealized oracle
rows.operation_detail: Fit oracle loss against aggregated parameter count on ensembles of 2 to 71 models, explored using iterative Pareto pruning.

conditions.value: 3,146 Pareto-optimal ensembles from combinations ranging from 2 to 71 models
fixed held-out text dataset sampled from D
per-text minimum summed token cross-entropy among pool models, normalized by average token sequence length across models and test texts
L(P) = A P^-α + L∞; nonlinear least squares in original loss domain

rows.note: The paper describes the ensemble frontier as exhibiting clear power-law scaling and reports an approximately 43% lower asymptotic floor than the single-model frontier. The fitted law is Lensemble(P) = 2.02/P^0.3502 + 1.25. This is an oracle lower bound, not a realizable ensemble result.
rows.check: Oracle per-text minimum loss over model ensembles, scaled by summed parameters. It is not a single language model's pretraining loss, so it bears on no version, including V7 (no fitting-choice or setup variation for single-model laws). Belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Pareto-optimal frontier of 12 public base LMs from 71, fixed held-out text, P up to ~80B
relationships.reason: R1: the single-model frontier fits L = 1.11 P^-0.3578 + 2.21, described as a 'clear power-law relationship'. The exponent is close to Chinchilla's. Support is weak because there are only 12 points, training data is uncontrolled and no fit statistics are given.
relationships.display_finding: The 12-model frontier fitted L = 1.11·P^−0.3578 + 2.21, with uncontrolled training data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Each reported frontier is fit with a power law in parameter count, and the paper describes the scaling behavior as clear or predictable (R1–R4). The test concerns parameter count and, for ensembles, oracle loss.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The fitted exponents and floors vary by frontier composition: in particular, same-family and cross-family pair fits differ, as do single-model and ensemble floors (R1–R4).
